newsitem.title: CHINA: China's Catholics, communists pray for HK.
newsitem.headline: China's Catholics, communists pray for HK.

text.p: China's Catholics prayed. Incense-burning Buddhists chanted sutras. So did the nation's atheist communist rulers, praying nothing goes wrong in the hours before Britain hands back the colony of Hong Kong.

About 500 Chinese Catholics flocked to the North Church, or the Hall of the Saviour built in 1703, in Beijing's Xishiku district on Sunday to attend morning mass and pray for a better tomorrow for Hong Kong, which reverts to Chinese rule at midnight (1600 GMT) on Monday.
At a Tibetan temple in Beijing, Buddhist faithful knelt, bowed and burned incense, while rows of monks clad in saffron robes chanted sutras against a backdrop of burning yak butter candles.
Beijing's streets are festooned with red lanterns and banners celebrating Hong Kong's return after more than 150 years of colonial rule, but behind the festive facade is fear.

In a sign of official nervousness, the Bureau of Religious Affairs banned reporters from interviewing church and temple-goers, fearful the faithful may say the wrong thing, make a slip or air a grievance.
Uniformed police and bureau officials patrolled the North Church, on alert against any untoward incident.
China regards Hong Kong's return as one of the events of the year -- if not the century -- and officials are obsessed with ensuring no domestic unrest ruffles the smooth handover.

The three million-strong People's Liberation Army and the police have been placed on high alert in Beijing and in parts of China such as restive Tibet and mainly Moslem Xinjiang amid fears of trouble in the run-up to the handover.
Police holidays have been cancelled and armed police now routinely stop cars, mainly taxis, at intersections to check motorists, demanding to see identification papers.
The Chinese capital and the restive northwestern Moslem region of Xinjiang have been rocked by bombings since February.
Authorities have launched a crackdown on underground religious activities in Xinjiang's Yili district, which was rocked by anti-Chinese riots last February.
Officials have stopped the unauthorised construction or renovation of 133 mosques, arrested 40 core participants in illegal religious activities and dispersed 105 illegal classes teaching the Koran.
The bombings have stunned the leadership, which has tried to put on a show of solidarity and stability after the death of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping on February 19.
For Pierre Fang, parish priest of the North Church, the return of Hong Kong reminded him of the passage in the Bible in which the shepherd finds his lost sheep.
"It's like Jesus saying in the Bible, he has 100 sheep, one was lost and he went to look for it," Fang said.
"This passage from the Bible reminds me that we must be very, very happy that a part of the motherland could return to its embrace," he said in an interview.
"We are celebrating Hong Kong's return in the holiest and most solemn way," Fang said. "We thank god... and we pray for peace."
